title: DOES FORGIVENESS MEAN LETTING THEM BACK IN? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD SET YOUR WOUNDED HEART FREE
paragraphs: DOES FORGIVENESS MEAN LETTING THEM BACK IN? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD SET YOUR WOUNDED HEART FREE

Jesus commanded you to forgive. But did He command you to trust the person who destroyed you? What Scripture actually says about forgiveness, reconciliation, repentance, and the boundaries that even love must respect.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from an enemy.
It comes from someone whose name used to make you smile.
Someone you prayed with. Someone you trusted with the parts of your life you never showed the world. Someone who knew exactly where you were vulnerable and somehow still chose to hurt you there.
And perhaps the cruelest part wasn't even what they did.
It was what happened afterward.
They wanted you to forgive them.
Immediately.
Without questions. Without accountability. Without allowing you time to grieve what their choices had destroyed.
Maybe they even opened a Bible.
Maybe they quoted Jesus.
Maybe they reminded you that Christians are supposed to forgive seventy times seven.
And suddenly, the person who wounded you was making you feel guilty for bleeding.
So you started asking yourself questions you were almost afraid to say aloud.
Am I disobeying God because I don't trust them anymore?
Am I bitter because I don't want them back in my life?
Does forgiving someone mean I have to pretend nothing happened?
And if I choose not to reconcile, will Jesus be disappointed in me?
If you've ever wrestled with those questions, stay with me.
Because there is a difference between refusing to forgive someone and refusing to give them another opportunity to destroy what God is healing.
And understanding that difference may change the way you carry your pain for the rest of your life.
But we need to be careful here.
Not every broken relationship should remain broken. Not every offender is beyond repentance. And not every boundary is necessarily righteous.
Sometimes pride disguises itself as protection.
Sometimes fear disguises itself as wisdom.
But sometimes what people call unforgiveness is actually a wounded person finally recognizing that love and trust are not the same thing.
We need more than comforting opinions to navigate this.
We need the Word of God.
And we need to let Jesus speak, even when His words challenge both the person who wounded us and the person who was wounded.
Because the Gospel does not merely teach us how to survive betrayal.
It teaches us what forgiveness really costs, what repentance really means, and why reconciliation cannot be built on a lie.
Consider something that happened nearly two thousand years ago.
A man named Jesus was hanging on a Roman cross.

His body had been scourged. His hands and feet were pierced. Soldiers had mocked Him. Religious leaders had rejected Him. One disciple had betrayed Him. Another had denied Him. Most of His closest followers had fled.
And while His enemies were still participating in His suffering, Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
— Luke 23:34, King James Version
The Greek text records His prayer as:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς· οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν.
Pater, aphes autois; ou gar oidasin ti poiousin.
"Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."
The verb ἄφες (aphes) comes from aphiēmi, a word that can mean to release, let go, remit, or forgive, depending on its context.
Jesus was not declaring that evil was harmless.
He was praying for mercy while enduring evil.
And that distinction matters.

There is also an important textual detail: Luke 23:34's prayer is included in many ancient manuscripts, including the traditional Greek text underlying the King James Version, but is absent from some other early manuscripts. Modern Bible editions sometimes mark it with a textual note. The prayer remains deeply consistent with Jesus' teaching to love enemies and pray for persecutors in Matthew 5:44.
Now notice something remarkable.

Jesus prayed for those responsible for His suffering, yet the New Testament does not teach that every person present at Calvary was automatically reconciled to God regardless of their response to Christ.
Peter later confronted his hearers about their involvement in Jesus' death and called them to repent and turn to God (Acts 3:13–19).
The offer of mercy was real.
The call to repentance was real.
And the need for a restored relationship with God was real.
This is where we must begin.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are profoundly connected, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness concerns our response to the wrong done against us.
Reconciliation concerns the restoration of a broken relationship.
Forgiveness can be offered even when the offender refuses to acknowledge the wrong.
Reconciliation, however, cannot become a truthful, healthy restoration while the offender continues denying the very harm that broke the relationship.
You can release your desire for revenge without restoring someone's access to your private life.
You can pray for a person without trusting them with your children.
You can genuinely desire someone's repentance without pretending that their behavior has changed.
And you can obey Christ's command to forgive while acknowledging that a relationship remains unsafe.
But please hear the other side.
Forgiveness is not merely saying, "I have moved on."
It is not simply blocking someone, forgetting their name, and convincing yourself you feel nothing.
Biblical forgiveness calls us away from vengeance, malice, and the desire to make another person suffer.
It invites us to entrust justice to God.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
Forgiveness does not mean that justice no longer matters.
It means you are not appointed to become your own instrument of revenge.
And sometimes that surrender is a battle.
Because when someone has deeply betrayed you, revenge can begin to feel like the only remaining evidence that your pain mattered.
You imagine the apology they never gave.
The confession they refuse to make.
The moment when everyone finally discovers what really happened.
You rehearse conversations in your mind.
You picture them understanding the damage.
And perhaps, in your most exhausted moments, you wish they could feel just a fraction of what you felt.
God sees that struggle.
But He does not want hatred to become the permanent tenant of a heart He purchased with the blood of His Son.
Forgiveness may begin as a trembling act of obedience long before your emotions catch up.
It may sound like:
"Lord, what they did was wrong. I will not call it good. I cannot pretend it didn't hurt. But I surrender my right to personal revenge. Teach me to forgive as You have forgiven me."
And tomorrow, when the memory returns, you may need to pray again.
That does not necessarily mean yesterday's prayer was dishonest.
Healing is not always instantaneous.
Sometimes forgiveness is a sincere decision that must be lived out repeatedly as old wounds surface.
But what happens when the person who hurt you wants back into your life?
This is where many Christians become confused.
They have heard Ephesians 4:32:
"And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."
And rightly so.
We are commanded to forgive.
But then they hear another passage.
Luke 17:3 says:
"Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him."
The Greek word translated "repent" is μετανοήσῃ (metanoēsē), from metanoeō, meaning to repent or change one's mind, with the biblical context calling for a genuine turning away from sin.
Notice that Jesus does not tell the injured person to pretend the offense never happened.
He says to rebuke the wrongdoing.
And He speaks of repentance.
One passage calls us to a forgiving heart. Another describes the role of repentance in responding to a brother or sister who sins.
These passages should not be forced into contradiction.

Christians may distinguish between an inward readiness to forgive and the relational granting of forgiveness in response to repentance. Different Christian traditions explain that distinction somewhat differently.
But the central biblical principles remain clear: believers must reject vengeance, pursue forgiveness, take repentance seriously, and never confuse restoration with the concealment of ongoing sin.
And genuine repentance is more than the words, "I'm sorry."
Sometimes people apologize because they miss your presence.
Sometimes because they dislike the consequences.
Sometimes because their reputation has been damaged.
Sometimes because they want the comfort of the relationship without the discomfort of accountability.
An apology can be sincere.
But an apology can also be a way of avoiding the truth.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 7:10:
"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death."
In context, Paul was addressing the Corinthians' response to correction. He then described the seriousness, eagerness, and desire to make things right that their godly sorrow had produced.
Godly sorrow does not merely regret being exposed.
It takes sin seriously.
That does not mean a repentant person becomes perfect overnight.
It means there is a genuine turning toward truth, accountability, and changed conduct.
Imagine a husband who has repeatedly betrayed his wife's trust.
He confesses.
He cries.
He asks forgiveness.
And perhaps his tears are genuine.
But can those tears alone rebuild what years of deception destroyed?
No.
Trust will require truthfulness, sustained faithfulness, accountability, and time.
His wife may choose to forgive him while still needing boundaries, counsel, and evidence of change.
Reconciliation may be possible.
But forgiveness does not require her to declare the marriage healed before the work of restoration has even begun.
And where abuse, coercion, or danger exists, safety must not be sacrificed to create the appearance of Christian unity.
The same principle applies beyond marriage.
The parent who repeatedly humiliates an adult child.
The friend who continually betrays confidences.
The church leader who manipulates people using spiritual authority.
The family member who refuses to stop abusive behavior.
The person who apologizes every time consequences arrive but returns to the same destructive pattern.
Christian love does not require us to call these patterns harmless.
In fact, biblical love demands truth.
First Corinthians 13:6 says that love:
"Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth."
Love does not celebrate wrongdoing.
And reconciliation that requires the injured person to deny reality is not biblical reconciliation.
It is a performance.
There is a passage that should stop every one of us from confusing forgiveness with automatic access.
John 2:24 says:
"But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men."
The Greek expression includes the verb ἐπίστευεν (episteuen), from pisteuō, which often means to believe, trust, or entrust.
In this context, John explains that Jesus did not entrust Himself to those around Him because He knew what was in humanity.
The immediate passage concerns people's response to His signs, not a direct teaching about abusive relationships.
So we should not misuse it as though Jesus were giving a modern boundary-setting seminar.
But the text does establish something important.
Jesus' perfect love did not mean indiscriminate personal trust.
He loved without sin.
He showed mercy without becoming naïve.
He knew the human heart.
And He did not entrust Himself to everyone.
Why, then, do we sometimes tell wounded Christians that genuine love requires them to trust someone whose behavior remains untrustworthy?
Wisdom is not the enemy of forgiveness.
Proverbs 22:3 says:
"A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished."
This is wisdom literature, not a command to withdraw from every difficult relationship.
But it plainly commends recognizing danger rather than recklessly ignoring it.
A boundary is not automatically an act of bitterness.
It may be an act of wisdom.
Of course, boundaries themselves must also be examined before God.
Are we establishing them to protect what is good, or to punish someone?
Are we seeking safety and integrity, or secretly hoping to control another person's emotions?
Are we leaving room for genuine repentance where restoration is appropriate?
The Holy Spirit does not merely examine the offender's heart.
He examines ours too.
And perhaps that is why this subject cuts so deeply.
Because some of us need permission to stop confusing forgiveness with self-abandonment.
While others need the courage to admit that we have been calling our resentment a boundary.
The Gospel confronts both.
Now consider Joseph.
If anyone had a human reason to hold a grudge, Joseph did.
His own brothers hated him.
They stripped him of his special robe.
They threw him into a pit.
They sold him into slavery.
Then they allowed their father to believe he was dead.
Imagine that betrayal.
Not from strangers.
From brothers.
People who shared his blood.
People who knew his childhood.
People who should have protected him.
Years passed.
Joseph suffered injustice, false accusation, imprisonment, and separation from his family.
And then, in one of the most extraordinary reversals in Scripture, the brothers who sold him stood before him in Egypt.
They needed food.
He held power.
They did not recognize him.
He recognized them.
Joseph could have destroyed them.
Instead, he eventually wept and revealed himself.
But read Genesis 42–45 carefully.
Joseph did not immediately disclose his identity and restore the family relationship at the first encounter.
The narrative includes a difficult process through which his brothers' attitudes and loyalties were brought into the open.
Judah, who had once participated in Joseph's sale, later offered himself in place of Benjamin.
Then Joseph revealed himself.
In Genesis 45:5, he told his brothers:
"Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life."
Joseph was not denying their wrongdoing.
He explicitly acknowledged that they had sold him.
Yet he also recognized God's providence.
And years later, after their father's death, the brothers feared that Joseph might finally retaliate.
Joseph answered in Genesis 50:20:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."
The Hebrew is especially powerful.
וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve'attem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
"You intended evil against me; God intended it for good."
The verb chashav appears in both halves of the statement, emphasizing the contrast between human intention and divine purpose.
Their intention was evil.
God's purpose was good.
Joseph did not say that their evil had secretly been righteous.
He said God had worked through what they intended for evil to accomplish a good purpose.
That is not the same thing.
And someone reading this needs to understand why.
God can redeem what happened to you without approving what happened to you.
He can bring beauty out of ashes without calling the fire beautiful.
He can use your testimony without having desired the sin that created your suffering.
And He can write a new chapter without requiring you to pretend the old one never existed.
But Joseph's story also contains a warning against simplistic conclusions.
Joseph and his brothers ultimately experienced reconciliation.
Their story should inspire hope that even severe family betrayal can be overcome through God's providence and changed relationships.
It should not be turned into a universal promise that every betrayer will repent or that every family relationship must be restored regardless of ongoing danger.
Scripture gives us another sobering example.
David was hunted by Saul.
Saul was the king.
David had served him.
Yet Saul repeatedly sought David's life.
In 1 Samuel 24, David had an opportunity to kill Saul but refused.
He would not take personal vengeance.
Saul acknowledged that David had treated him more righteously.
Yet David did not simply return to Saul's household and behave as though the danger had vanished.
The chapter ends with Saul going home and David returning to the stronghold.
David's restraint was real.
His refusal to retaliate was real.
And his continued caution was real.
Later, Saul again pursued David.
The narrative does not present David's mercy as foolishness, nor does it demand that mercy erase discernment.
You can refuse revenge and still take danger seriously.
You can desire someone's good and still remain at a distance.
And sometimes the most loving thing you can do is stop enabling the behavior that is destroying them and everyone around them.
Yet we must not stop with Joseph and David.
Because forgiveness is not ultimately about proving that we were right and someone else was wrong.
It is about the God who forgave sinners through Jesus Christ.
And here the Gospel becomes uncomfortable for all of us.
Because at some point, we have to stop seeing ourselves only as the wounded person.
We also have to recognize ourselves as sinners who need mercy.
Perhaps you have never betrayed someone as Joseph's brothers did.
Perhaps you have never persecuted someone as Saul persecuted David.
But have you ever lied?
Have you ever wounded someone with words?
Have you ever withheld an apology because admitting the truth would cost you your pride?
Have you ever expected grace for your failures while demanding perfection from everyone else?
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
All.
Not only the person who hurt you.
Not only the person you refuse to speak to.
You.
Me.
Every one of us.
And this is why the cross must remain at the center of every conversation about forgiveness.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make wounded people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
Colossians 1:20 speaks of God's work through Christ:
"And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself..."
The Greek verb ἀποκαταλλάξαι (apokatallaxai) expresses reconciliation, the restoration of a relationship of peace.
In its context, this is God's cosmic work through Christ, not a guarantee that every human relationship will be restored in this present life.
But it reveals the heart of the Gospel.
Sin created alienation.
Christ made peace through His blood.
We do not reconcile ourselves to God through good behavior, religious performance, or the illusion that we were never guilty.
We are reconciled through Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:18 says:
"And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation."
This ministry matters.
Christians should be people who seek peace, pursue truth, welcome repentance, and work toward restoration whenever it is righteous and possible.
We should never celebrate broken relationships merely because reconciliation would require humility.
We should not cling to grudges because they make us feel powerful.
We should not close our hearts to someone who has genuinely repented simply because forgiveness is difficult.
But neither should we use the ministry of reconciliation to force an injured person back into an unsafe relationship.
Romans 12:18 gives us a beautifully honest instruction:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
As much as lieth in you.
Paul commands believers to pursue peace while acknowledging that peaceful relationships are not always within one person's power.
You cannot repent on someone else's behalf.
You cannot force someone to tell the truth.
You cannot manufacture another person's integrity.
You cannot create mutual trust alone.
You can obey God in your own conduct.
You can confess your own sin.
You can seek peace.
You can pray.
You can forgive.
But you cannot control whether another person chooses repentance.
And this brings us to a painful truth.
Sometimes the relationship you are grieving is not merely the relationship you lost.
It is the relationship you thought you had.
You are mourning the parent you needed.
The spouse you believed you married.
The friend you thought would never betray you.
The spiritual leader you trusted to protect you.
The version of someone that existed in your hopes long after their actions began telling a different story.
And sometimes you are not struggling to forgive what happened.
You are struggling to accept that it happened at all.
That is grief.
And grief deserves honesty before God.
The Psalms show us that faithful people can bring anguish, confusion, anger, and tears into God's presence.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
You do not need to manufacture a smile to be heard by God.
You do not need to minimize your suffering to demonstrate spiritual maturity.
And you do not need to call an unsafe relationship safe in order to prove that Jesus lives in your heart.
But do not mistake distance for healing either.
You can be miles away from someone and still let resentment dominate every thought.
You can establish a necessary boundary while continuing to pray that God will deal justly and mercifully with the other person.
And if bitterness has taken root, you can bring that too before Christ.
Hebrews 12:15 warns about a root of bitterness springing up and troubling many.
Bitterness can spread through our speech, relationships, and understanding of the world.
The wrong done to you may not have been your choice.
But what you cultivate in response still matters.
Do not let someone else's sin become the justification for your own.
And please understand that this warning must never be weaponized against victims.
A person who reports abuse, seeks legal protection, tells the truth, or refuses unsafe contact is not automatically bitter.
Justice and forgiveness are not enemies.
Accountability and mercy are not opposites.
A Christian can forgive while cooperating with legitimate investigations, pursuing appropriate legal remedies, or protecting vulnerable people from further harm.
Indeed, where children or other vulnerable people face danger, protective action may be a moral responsibility.
No church leader, family member, or ministry has biblical authority to demand silence about abuse in the name of forgiveness.
And no one should be pressured to meet privately with a dangerous offender to prove spiritual maturity.
Reconciliation is not a license for repeated harm.
Now perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
You are not the person who was betrayed.
You are the one who betrayed someone's trust.
You have apologized.
You have asked for another chance.
You have told them you have changed.
But they still keep their distance.
And you are angry because you believe that if they truly forgave you, everything would return to normal.
Please listen carefully.
Their forgiveness does not erase the consequences of your choices.
Repentance does not entitle you to immediate trust.
You cannot demand restoration as payment for an apology.
If you are genuinely repentant, you must be willing to tell the truth, accept accountability, respect appropriate boundaries, and demonstrate change without controlling the outcome.
You may have to accept that the relationship will never return to what it was.
And that does not mean God's grace has failed.
It means forgiveness is not the same as entitlement.
Remember Zacchaeus.
When Jesus entered his life, Zacchaeus responded with a willingness to give generously and restore what he had wrongfully taken.
Luke 19:8 records his declaration that he would restore fourfold if he had taken anything by false accusation.
Restitution was not the price by which he purchased salvation.
It was evidence of a transformed response to Jesus.
Grace did not make his wrongdoing irrelevant.
Grace changed the way he dealt with it.
And if you have harmed someone, that is the kind of repentance worth pursuing.
Not merely, "How can I get them back?"
But, "Lord, how must I change, even if they never come back?"
Because repentance that exists only to recover access is not the same as repentance that desires holiness.
And to the person who has been wounded, there is something equally important you need to hear.
Do not let the fear of being hurt again become a vow that nobody will ever be allowed close to you.
Not everyone is your betrayer.
Not every disagreement is manipulation.
Not every imperfect person is dangerous.
Discernment protects the heart.
Fear can imprison it.
And Jesus is able to teach us the difference.
Sometimes reconciliation begins with a difficult conversation.
Sometimes it begins with a confession.
Sometimes it requires a long season of changed behavior.
Sometimes wise pastoral counsel, professional counseling, or appropriate accountability can help.
Sometimes reconciliation is limited: two people can acknowledge the past, release hostility, and interact peacefully without returning to their former closeness.
And sometimes, because of ongoing danger or refusal to repent, a close relationship cannot responsibly be restored.
The goal is not to force every story into the same ending.
The goal is to honor Christ in the story you have actually been given.
And if you are wondering whether you have truly forgiven someone, do not measure forgiveness only by whether you can sit across a table from them without trembling.
Ask whether you are willing to surrender vengeance to God.
Ask whether you can desire their genuine repentance rather than their destruction.
Ask whether your boundaries serve truth and protection rather than cruelty.
Ask whether you are willing for God to examine your own heart.
And ask whether you are allowing Jesus to heal you instead of making your wound the permanent center of your identity.
Because you are more than what happened to you.
You are not merely the person who was abandoned.
Not merely the person who was betrayed.
Not merely the child who was rejected.
Not merely the believer who was disappointed by someone in the church.
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not determined by another person's sin.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That does not mean every traumatic memory instantly disappears.
It does not mean every relationship is restored.
It means that in Christ, your life has a new foundation.
Your past is real.
But it is not your lord.
Your wounds are real.
But they are not your savior.
Jesus Christ is.
And there is one more thing I want you to consider.
At the cross, Jesus did not minimize sin to make forgiveness possible.
He bore its cost.
God's mercy is not moral indifference.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing greatness of divine grace.
That is why forgiveness is never something to treat cheaply.
And that is why reconciliation must never be built on pretending that truth does not matter.
Perhaps today you need to forgive someone you have secretly been punishing in your heart.
Perhaps you need to repent because you have been demanding trust you have not rebuilt.
Perhaps you need to stop calling necessary protection a lack of faith.
Perhaps you need to humble yourself and seek reconciliation with someone who has genuinely repented.
Or perhaps you need to accept that you cannot heal a relationship alone.
Whatever your situation, do not make your next decision merely to escape discomfort.
Bring it to Jesus.
Search the Scriptures.
Seek wise and trustworthy counsel where needed.
Tell the truth.
Reject revenge.
Honor repentance.
Protect the vulnerable.
Pursue peace as far as it depends on you.
And refuse to make another person's response the measure of your obedience to God.
Because the most beautiful part of this story is not that every person who hurt you will return transformed.
Some may never apologize.
Some may never understand.
Some may never acknowledge the tears you cried because of them.
The beautiful part is that Jesus can transform your heart even when someone else refuses to change.
He can teach you to forgive without denying the truth.
To love without surrendering wisdom.
To hope without demanding a particular outcome.
To grieve without losing faith.
And to move forward without carrying revenge as your companion.
That is not weakness.
That is grace working in a human heart.
And it brings us back to the very heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because every consequence disappears.
Not because forgiveness magically restores every broken relationship.
But because the risen Christ is greater than our sin, our shame, our betrayal, and our deepest wounds.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
He restores people to God.
And He continues transforming those who belong to Him.
Maybe the person you have been waiting for will never say, "I'm sorry."
But you can still bring your broken heart to the Savior who knows what betrayal feels like.
And maybe you are the one who needs to say those words.
If so, do not wait for another excuse.
Repent.
Confess.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Seek forgiveness without demanding reconciliation.
And let the Gospel change more than your vocabulary.
Let it change your life.
Before you leave this article, I want to invite you to be honest.
Not with the version of yourself that knows how to look strong in public.
With the part of you that still remembers.
The part that still struggles.
The part that still needs Jesus.
Your story may help someone believe that change is possible.
You do not need to reveal private details or identify anyone who hurt you.
God knows the story, even when you cannot safely tell the whole world.
And if this message helped you understand forgiveness in a way you never have before, please do not let it end with you.
There may be someone scrolling through their feed tonight who is silently struggling under the weight of religious guilt, believing that God requires them to return to an unsafe relationship.
There may also be someone who has been using the language of boundaries to avoid the hard work of forgiveness.
Both need the truth.
Both need Jesus.
Because the world does not need more shallow religious slogans.
It needs people who will open the Bible, face the truth, and follow Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Jesus, I want to invite you to take another step.
Not because supporting this particular ministry is a biblical requirement.
And certainly not because your giving can replace the faithful stewardship, generosity, and responsibilities you already have before God.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Cheerfully.
Christ is our Savior.

Help us bring these conversations about repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation beyond the walls of a church building and into the lives of people who may have stopped believing that Jesus still cares about their pain.
Because this is not ultimately about growing a page.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
And if even one person reads this message, turns away from sin, seeks Christ, and begins walking in the truth, that is something worth thanking God for.
Now, before you close this, I want to leave you with one final thought.
You may never receive the apology you deserved.
You may never recover the relationship you lost.
You may never understand why someone who claimed to love you chose to wound you so deeply.
But the story of your life is not finished at the moment someone betrayed you.
There is a Savior who was betrayed with a kiss.
A Savior who was denied by a friend.
A Savior who carried a cross He did not deserve.
A Savior who died for sinners and rose again so that all who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
Bring your wounds to Him.
Bring your sins to Him.
Bring your unanswered questions to Him.
And when the road toward forgiveness feels longer than you expected, remember that His grace is not exhausted by your weakness.
You do not have to reopen the door to the person who broke your heart to open your heart completely to the Jesus who can make you whole.
